Ch 1: Fluid Properties & Pressure

Lecture 1.1 · Text Ch 1.1–1.7 · Week of May 4th

1.1 — Introduction

Fluid mechanics studies how fluids (liquids and gases) behave at rest and in motion. It is one of the most broadly applicable areas in engineering — spanning aerodynamics, marine propulsion, biomedical devices, renewable energy, sports engineering, and environmental science. In this course, we develop governing equations using the control volume approach and apply them to practical engineering problems.

Applications of Fluid Mechanics

The reach of fluid mechanics is enormous. Some representative domains:

Transportation — helicopter vortex ring states, ship propeller vortices, CFD streamline simulations for race car aerodynamics. Understanding lift, drag, and flow separation is central to vehicle design across aviation, marine, and automotive engineering.

Biomedical — computational fluid dynamics for artificial heart pump design (modeling blood flow through impellers), lung airflow simulation through branching airways, arterial blood flow modeling for detecting aneurysms and stenosis.

Energy — water flow simulation in hydroelectric dams (velocity magnitude fields through spillways), airflow through wind turbine blades (vortex shedding and wake interactions), combustion chamber flows in gas turbines.

Environment & Geophysics — ocean current modeling for climate prediction, atmospheric pollution dispersion driven by wind patterns.

Sports — aerodynamic drag optimization of golf club heads, bobsled body shaping, cyclist helmet streamlining — all use CFD velocity field analysis to minimize drag coefficients.

The Concept of a Fluid: Classification of Matter

Matter exists in four states — solid, liquid, gas, and plasma. In this course, we focus on liquids and gases, which are collectively called fluids. The critical distinction between solids and fluids comes down to how they respond to shear stress.

Classification of matter by state. Liquids and gases are collectively called fluids.
Solid

Molecules are packed in a lattice or geometric structure with constant molecular spacing. Large cohesive forces hold molecules together, preventing relative movement except for slight vibration. When subjected to a load, a solid deforms but continues to support the load — internal shear stresses build up and reach equilibrium. A solid can resist shear stress by deforming.

Liquid

Molecules are not bound in a lattice — they are more mobile than in solids, but molecular spacing is still approximately constant. Liquids do not hold their shape; they flow and take the shape of their container, forming a horizontal free surface at the top. When confined, their intermolecular forces allow them to resist compressive forces, so liquids have constant volume and density. However, they cannot resist shear loading — instead of reaching equilibrium, they deform continuously and form waves (think of coffee sloshing in a mug).

Gas

Intermolecular forces are weak enough to allow molecules to travel freely until repelled by other molecules. Gases have no definite volume — they must be held in a container, otherwise they flow out to form an atmosphere. A gas completely fills any space it occupies. Gravitational effects are negligible compared to buoyancy forces. Gases are still classified as fluids because they flow when subjected to a force (e.g., gas flow in pipes).

A fourth state, plasma (ionized matter), exists and is critical for fusion energy research (e.g., tokamak reactors), but it is not covered in MAAE 2300.

Common examples to keep in mind: Solids — steel, aluminum, wood. Liquids — water, alcohol, oil. Gases — oxygen, nitrogen, air.

★ Key Distinction: Solid vs Fluid

A solid resists shear stress by deforming to a static equilibrium — loading causes internal shear stresses that balance the applied force. A fluid cannot resist any shear stress — it deforms continuously under even the smallest applied shear, no matter how small. This continuous deformation under shear is the defining property of a fluid. Note: this does not mean fluids have no viscosity — viscous effects resist the rate of deformation, but the fluid never reaches static equilibrium under shear.

The Concept of Continuum

At the molecular level, matter is discrete — individual molecules bouncing around with gaps between them. But in engineering, we want to treat fluid properties like density as smooth, continuous functions so we can use calculus. The continuum assumption makes this possible.

Consider measuring density by counting mass in a sample volume of size \(\delta V\):

Case 1: Volume comparable to intermolecular spacing (very small \(\delta V\)). The number of molecules inside fluctuates wildly as they move in and out. The measured density \(\rho = \delta m / \delta V\) is noisy and unstable — this is microscopic uncertainty.

Case 2: Volume much larger than intermolecular spacing. The number of molecules entering roughly equals the number leaving at any instant. The measured density stabilizes to a constant value — fluctuations average out. This is the continuum regime.

Case 3: Volume too large (macroscopic scale). The density starts reflecting spatial variations across the fluid (e.g., a container with sloshing, spilling fluid) rather than a local point value — this is macroscopic uncertainty.

Density (Continuum Definition)

\[ \rho = \lim_{\delta V \to \delta V^*} \frac{\delta m}{\delta V} \]

\(\rho\) — density (kg/m³) \(\delta m\) — mass in volume element (kg) \(\delta V\) — volume element (m³) \(\delta V^*\) — smallest volume for stable density (~\(10^{-9}\) mm³)

When to use: Any problem requiring fluid density as a point property — underlies every governing equation in this course (continuity, momentum, energy).

When NOT to use: Rarefied gas flows (high altitude, vacuum systems) where the mean free path approaches the characteristic length of the problem. In those cases, molecular dynamics or kinetic theory is needed instead.

Density measured as a function of sample volume δV. Below δV*, molecular fluctuations dominate. Above δV*, density stabilizes — this is the continuum regime. At very large volumes, spatial non-uniformity introduces macroscopic uncertainty.

At standard atmospheric conditions, \(\delta V^*_{\text{air}}\) contains approximately \(3 \times 10^7\) molecules — a sufficiently large number for a stable statistical average. Since \(\delta V^*\) is extremely small compared to any engineering dimension, density (and all other fluid properties) can be treated as smoothly varying functions of position.

★ Why Continuum Matters

The continuum assumption is what lets us write partial derivatives, integrals, and governing PDEs for fluid flow. Every equation in Ch 3–6 (continuity, momentum, energy, Bernoulli) relies on density, velocity, and pressure being differentiable functions of space and time. Without continuum, we would need molecular dynamics — computationally impractical for engineering-scale problems.

Branches of Fluid Mechanics

The field is divided into three branches, each of which we study in this course:

The three branches of fluid mechanics and their corresponding chapters in this course.
Hydrostatics

The study of fluids at rest or moving with constant velocity (no acceleration). Covers pressure distribution, forces on submerged surfaces, and buoyancy. Focus of Ch 1–2.

Kinematics

The study of the geometry of fluid motion — velocity fields, streamlines, pathlines, and streaklines — without considering the forces that cause the motion. Covered beginning in Ch 4.

Fluid Dynamics

The study of the forces that cause accelerated motion in fluids. This is where we develop and apply the momentum and energy equations using the Reynolds Transport Theorem (Ch 5–6).

1.2 — Units, Dimensional Analysis & Fluid Properties

Dimensions and Units

To describe the physical state of a fluid quantitatively, we need two concepts: dimensions (the measure by which a physical variable is expressed) and units (a particular way of attaching a number to that dimension). We use curly braces { } to denote dimensions and square brackets [ ] to denote units.

Dimension

The measure by which a physical variable is expressed quantitatively. For example, the dimension of the height of a fluid container is Length {L}.

Unit

A particular way of attaching a number to a quantitative dimension. For example, the unit of the dimension of length in the metric system is the meter [m].

Primary Dimensions

In fluid mechanics, four primary (independent) dimensions form the foundation from which all other quantities are derived:

DimensionSymbol
Mass{M}
Length{L}
Time{T}
Temperature{Θ}

A fifth primary dimension, Electric Current {I}, exists for electrically conducting fluids like liquid metals and electrolytes, but it is not used in this course. All other physical properties are derived from these four primaries. For example, force comes from Newton’s second law:

Dimension of Force

\[ \mathbf{F} = m \cdot \mathbf{a} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \{F\} = \{MLT^{-2}\} \]

F = force m = mass {M} a = acceleration {LT−2}

Systems of Units

Two primary unit systems are used in this course:

DimensionSIBG (British Gravitational)
MassKilogram [kg]Slug
LengthMeter [m]Foot [ft]
TimeSecond [s]Second [s]
TemperatureKelvin [K]Rankine [°R]

Both SI and BG require no proportionality constants — Newton’s second law is simply \(\mathbf{F} = m \cdot \mathbf{a}\). Conversion between the two systems uses:

SI ↔ BG Conversions

\[ 1\;\text{slug} = 14.5939\;\text{kg} \qquad 1\;\text{ft} = 0.3048\;\text{m} \qquad 1\;\text{K} = 1.8\;{^\circ\text{R}} \]

This gives the force conversion: \(1\;\text{N} = 1\;\text{kg}\!\cdot\!\text{m}\!\cdot\!\text{s}^{-2} = 0.224809\;\text{lbf}\)

lbf = pound-force (BG force unit) 1 lbf = 1 slug·ft·s−2

Secondary (Derived) Dimensions

All other physical quantities used in fluid mechanics are derived from the four primary dimensions. The table below shows the most important ones with their SI and BG units and conversion factors:

QuantityDimensionSI unitBG unitConversion
Area{L²}m²ft²1 m² = 10.764 ft²
Volume{L³}m³ft³1 m³ = 35.315 ft³
Velocity{LT−1}m/sft/s1 ft/s = 0.3048 m/s
Acceleration{LT−2}m/s²ft/s²1 ft/s² = 0.3048 m/s²
Pressure / stress{ML−1T−2}Pa = N/m²lbf/ft²1 lbf/ft² = 47.88 Pa
Energy / work{ML²T−2}J = N·mft·lbf1 ft·lbf = 1.3558 J
Power{ML²T−3}W = J/sft·lbf/s1 ft·lbf/s = 1.3558 W
Density{ML−3}kg/m³slugs/ft³1 slug/ft³ = 515.4 kg/m³
Viscosity{ML−1T−1}kg/(m·s)slugs/(ft·s)1 slug/(ft·s) = 47.88 kg/(m·s)

Other Unit Systems

The CGS (Centimeter-Gram-Second) system uses cm, g, and s as primary units. Its unit of force is the dyne: \(1\;\text{dyne} = 1\;\text{g}\!\cdot\!\text{cm}\!\cdot\!\text{s}^{-2} = 10^{-5}\;\text{N}\). CGS requires no proportionality constants, but its units are too small for most engineering applications — the weight of a nickel is about 4900 dynes!

The English Engineering System (lbf, lbm, ft, s, °R) uses a proportionality constant \(g_c\) in Newton’s second law: \(\mathbf{F} = \frac{m \cdot \mathbf{a}}{g_c}\) where \(g_c = 32.174\;\text{lbm/slug}\). This extra constant is why we prefer SI and BG — they keep \(\mathbf{F} = m \cdot \mathbf{a}\) clean. The relation is \(1\;\text{slug} = 32.174\;\text{lbm}\).

SI Prefixes

Powers of 10 provide a compact way to express very large or very small values. Memorize at least kilo (10³), mega (10⁶), giga (10⁹), milli (10−³), micro (10−⁶), and nano (10−⁹).

FactorPrefixSymbolFactorPrefixSymbol
10¹²teraT10−¹decid
10⁹gigaG10−²centic
10⁶megaM10−³millim
10³kilok10−⁶microμ
10²hectoh10−⁹nanon
10dekada10−¹²picop

Examples: \(114{,}000{,}000\;\text{Pa} \equiv 114\;\text{MPa}\) and \(0.000000003\;\text{s} \equiv 3\;\text{ns}\).

Consistency and Homogeneity

★ Three Rules for Unit Consistency

Rule 1: Never mix BG and SI units. Select one system and convert everything to it before computing.
Example: \(1\;\text{slug} + 1\;\text{kg} \to 14.5939\;\text{kg} + 1\;\text{kg} = 15.5939\;\text{kg}\)

Rule 2: Never mix prefixes when adding or subtracting. Convert to the same power of 10.
Example: \(0.1\;\text{MPa} + 10{,}000\;\text{Pa} = 100{,}000\;\text{Pa} + 10{,}000\;\text{Pa} = 110{,}000\;\text{Pa}\)

Rule 3: Never use dimensionally inconsistent equations. Adding force and velocity is nonsense:
\(\{F\} + \{V\} = \text{nonsense} \equiv \{MLT^{-2}\} + \{LT^{-1}\}\)

Principle of Dimensional Homogeneity

Every term in a valid equation must have the same dimensions. Consider Bernoulli’s equation (derived in Ch 3):

Dimensional Check — Bernoulli’s Equation

\[ p + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2 + \rho g Z = \text{constant} \]

Check each term:

\(\{p\} = \{ML^{-1}T^{-2}\}\)

\(\{\tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2\} = \{ML^{-3}\} \cdot \{LT^{-1}\}^2 = \{ML^{-1}T^{-2}\}\) ✓

\(\{\rho g Z\} = \{ML^{-3}\} \cdot \{LT^{-2}\} \cdot \{L\} = \{ML^{-1}T^{-2}\}\) ✓

All terms have dimensions \(\{ML^{-1}T^{-2}\}\) — dimensionally consistent.

Some manufacturer-quoted formulas appear dimensionally inconsistent at first glance. For example, a valve flow coefficient \(Q = C_V \sqrt{\Delta p / SG}\) looks inconsistent because \(C_V\) carries hidden dimensions \(\{L^{7/2} M^{-1/2}\}\) to make the equation work. Always check whether “constants” carry dimensions.

Fluid Properties: Overview

Fluid properties are classified into two categories:

Extensive Properties

Properties that depend on the total amount of fluid (total mass of the system). Typically represented by uppercase letters. Examples: Mass \(M\), Weight \(W\), Volume \(\mathcal{V}\).

Intensive Properties

Properties that are independent of the amount of fluid — they describe the state at a point. Typically represented by lowercase letters. Examples: Density \(\rho\), Pressure \(p\), Temperature \(T\).

Pressure and Stress

Stress is force per unit area. There are two kinds relevant to fluids:

Normal stress acts perpendicular to a surface. Tensile stress (pulling apart): \(\sigma_{\text{tensile}} = +F/A\). Compressive stress (pushing together): \(\sigma_{\text{compressive}} = -F/A\). Recall from Sec. 1.1 that fluids cannot resist shear stresses — they deform continuously under any applied shear \(\tau = F/A\).

Pressure

Pressure is the compressive normal force per unit area acting on a fluid element. Using the continuum assumption, at a point:

\[ p = \lim_{\Delta A \to 0} \frac{\Delta F}{\Delta A} = \frac{dF}{dA} \]

For a finite area with uniform pressure: \(p_{\text{avg}} = F/A\)

p = pressure F = normal force A = area SI: Pa = N/m² BG: psf = lbf/ft² or psi = lbf/in²
★ Pressure in a Static Fluid

In a static fluid, pressure acts equally in all directions at a point (Pascal’s law). The shear stress is zero: \(\tau = 0\). Pressure is a scalar — it has magnitude but no direction. The compressive normal stress equals the negative of pressure: \(-\sigma = p\).

Density

Density

\[ \rho = \frac{m}{V} \]

Mass of the fluid contained in a unit volume.

ρ = density m = mass V = volume SI: kg/m³ BG: slugs/ft³

Liquids are nearly incompressible — density varies little with pressure. It varies slightly more with temperature: \(\rho_{\text{water}}\) at 4°C is 1000 kg/m³ but drops to 958.1 kg/m³ at 100°C. For small temperature ranges, density change is typically negligible.

Gases are compressible — their density changes significantly with both pressure and temperature. The ideal gas law (covered later in this lecture) governs this relationship.

Specific Weight

Specific Weight

\[ \gamma = \frac{W}{V} = \rho g \]

Weight of the fluid per unit volume. Since \(W = mg\) and \(V = m/\rho\), we get \(\gamma = \rho g\).

γ = specific weight W = weight ρ = density g = gravitational acceleration SI: N/m³ BG: lbf/ft³

Specific Gravity

Specific Gravity

\[ SG = \frac{\rho}{\rho_W} = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma_W} \]

Ratio of a fluid’s density to that of the reference: water at 4°C and 101.3 kPa. \(\rho_W = 1000\;\text{kg/m}^3 \equiv 62.4\;\text{lbf/ft}^3\)

SG = specific gravity (dimensionless) ρW = density of water at 4°C
★ Specific Gravity in Practice

SG is dimensionless — the same number in SI and BG. \(SG > 1\) means the fluid is denser than water (it sinks); \(SG < 1\) means it floats. Mercury: \(SG \approx 13.6\); gasoline: \(SG \approx 0.68\).

Bulk Modulus

Bulk Modulus

\[ E_V = -\frac{dp}{dV/V} \]

A measure of how much a fluid resists compression. As pressure increases (\(dp > 0\)), volume decreases (\(dV < 0\)), so the negative sign makes \(E_V\) positive. Has dimensions of pressure.

EV = bulk modulus dp = change in pressure dV/V = volumetric strain SI: Pa

Liquids have very high \(E_V\) — nearly incompressible. Gases have very low \(E_V\) — easily compressed. This is why we often treat liquids as incompressible (\(\rho = \text{const}\)) in this course.

Temperature

Temperature Conversions

\[ {^\circ\text{R}} = {^\circ\text{F}} + 459.69 \qquad \text{K} = {^\circ\text{C}} + 273.16 \qquad {^\circ\text{C}} = ({^\circ\text{F}} - 32) \times \tfrac{5}{9} \]

K and °R are absolute scales 0 K = absolute zero = 0 °R

Viscosity

Recall from Sec. 1.1 that fluids cannot resist shear forces — they deform continuously. But how fast they deform depends on the fluid. Water layers slide past each other quickly under shear; maple syrup layers move much more slowly. The property that quantifies this resistance to flow is viscosity.

Imagine a fluid confined between a fixed lower surface and a moving upper plate. When a force \(F\) is applied to the plate, it drags the fluid along. The fluid in contact with the moving plate moves at the plate’s velocity (\(u = V\) at the top), while the fluid in contact with the fixed surface is stationary (\(u = 0\) at the bottom). This creates a velocity gradient across the gap — thin layers of fluid slide over each other. Viscosity causes internal friction, leading to energy loss.

Newton’s law of viscosity. Left: deformation of a fluid element under shear. Center: velocity profile u(y) between plates. Right: Couette flow setup with no-slip condition at both surfaces.

The shear angle \(\delta\theta\) relates to velocity displacement: \(\delta\theta \approx \tan\delta\theta = \delta u \cdot \delta t / \delta y\). Taking limits gives the strain rate \(d\theta/dt = du/dy\). The shear stress is proportional to this strain rate:

Newton’s Law of Viscosity

\[ \tau = \mu \frac{du(y)}{dy} \]

The shear stress in a fluid is proportional to the velocity gradient (rate of shear strain). The constant of proportionality \(\mu\) is the dynamic (absolute) viscosity.

τ = shear stress μ = dynamic viscosity du/dy = velocity gradient (strain rate) SI: N·s/m² = Pa·s BG: lbf·s/ft²
No-Slip Condition

At any solid boundary, the fluid velocity equals the surface velocity. At a stationary wall: \(u = 0\). At a moving plate with speed \(V\): \(u = V\). This is a fundamental boundary condition in fluid mechanics, observed experimentally for all viscous fluids in contact with solid surfaces.

Newtonian vs Non-Newtonian Fluids

Newtonian Fluid

A fluid with constant viscosity regardless of the applied shear stress. The \(\tau\) vs \(du/dy\) plot is a straight line through the origin with slope \(\mu\). Examples: air, water, gasoline, mercury, crude oil. The steeper the line, the higher the viscosity and the harder the fluid is to move.

Classification of fluid behavior. Newtonian fluids: linear τ vs dθ/dt. Non-Newtonian: dilatant (slope increases), pseudoplastic (slope decreases), and Bingham plastic (yield stress required to start flow).
Non-Newtonian Fluids

Fluids with a nonlinear shear stress vs. strain rate relationship. The apparent viscosity (slope at any point) changes with shear rate:

Dilatant (shear-thickening): Viscosity increases with strain rate. Example: water with high sugar concentration.

Pseudoplastic (shear-thinning): Viscosity decreases with strain rate. Examples: ketchup, gelatin, blood.

Ideal Bingham plastic: Requires a yield stress before deformation begins, then behaves linearly. Example: toothpaste.

Effect of Temperature on Viscosity

Viscosity changes only slightly with pressure (generally neglected). It is strongly temperature-dependent:

Liquids: Viscosity decreases with temperature. Higher T increases molecular vibration, breaking intermolecular bonds and allowing layers to slide more easily.

Gases: Viscosity increases with temperature. Higher T brings weakly bonded molecules closer during collisions, enhancing momentum exchange between layers.

Variation of dynamic (absolute) viscosity with temperature at 1 atm. Liquids (top curves) decrease with T; gases (bottom curves) increase with T. Note the log scale.
Empirical Viscosity–Temperature Relations

Liquids (Andrade’s equation): \(\;\mu = B \, e^{C/T}\)

Gases (Sutherland equation): \(\;\mu = \dfrac{B \, T^{3/2}}{T + C}\)

where \(T\) is absolute temperature; \(B\) and \(C\) are constants determined from known viscosities at specific temperatures.

T = absolute temperature [K or °R] B, C = empirical constants (fluid-specific)

Kinematic Viscosity

Kinematic Viscosity

\[ \nu = \frac{\mu}{\rho} \]

Called “kinematic” because force is not involved in its dimensions — only length and time.

ν = kinematic viscosity μ = dynamic viscosity ρ = density SI: m²/s BG: ft²/s
★ Dynamic vs Kinematic Viscosity

Dynamic viscosity \(\mu\) is used in Newton’s law of viscosity when shear forces matter. Kinematic viscosity \(\nu\) appears in dimensionless numbers like the Reynolds number \(Re = VL/\nu\) (Ch 4–6). Mercury has high \(\mu\) but low \(\nu\) because of its very high density.

Inviscid and Ideal Fluids

Inviscid Fluid

A fluid with zero viscosity (\(\mu = 0\)). Many engineering fluids have very low viscosity — at 20°C: \(\mu_{\text{water}} = 10^{-3}\;\text{N}\!\cdot\!\text{s/m}^2\), \(\mu_{\text{air}} = 1.81 \times 10^{-5}\;\text{N}\!\cdot\!\text{s/m}^2\).

Ideal Fluid

A fluid that is both inviscid (\(\mu = 0\)) and incompressible (\(\rho = \text{const}\)). This is the simplest fluid model and underlies Bernoulli’s equation (Ch 3).

Worked Example: Determining Viscosity

Example — Viscosity from Plate Experiment

Problem: A plate moves at 0.6 mm/s with an applied force of 4 mN. Contact area is 0.5 m², gap is 4 mm. Assuming a linear velocity profile, find the viscosity.

Solution

Step 1 — Shear stress:

\[ \tau = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{4 \times 10^{-3}\;\text{N}}{0.5\;\text{m}^2} = 8.0 \times 10^{-3}\;\text{N/m}^2 \]

Step 2 — Velocity gradient (linear profile ⇒ constant):

\[ \frac{du}{dy} = \frac{V}{h} = \frac{0.6 \times 10^{-3}\;\text{m/s}}{4 \times 10^{-3}\;\text{m}} = 0.15\;\text{s}^{-1} \]

Step 3 — Apply Newton’s law:

\[ \mu = \frac{\tau}{du/dy} = \frac{8.0 \times 10^{-3}}{0.15} = \boxed{0.0533\;\text{N}\!\cdot\!\text{s/m}^2} \]

Surface Tension and Capillarity

Cohesion and Adhesion

Cohesion: The attractive force between molecules of the same liquid. Enables a liquid to maintain its form.

Adhesion: The attractive force between liquid molecules and the molecules of a different material (e.g., the container wall).

At a liquid surface, molecules are pulled inward by cohesive forces from neighbors below but have no liquid neighbors above. The net force is directed downward into the bulk, causing the surface to contract like a stretched elastic membrane.

Surface Tension

\[ \Upsilon = \frac{F}{L} \]

Force per unit length needed to separate surface molecules. Also interpreted as free-surface energy (work per increase in surface area). Temperature-dependent — \(\Upsilon\) decreases as temperature rises.

Υ = surface tension SI: N/m BG: lbf/ft

Pressure Inside a Liquid Droplet

Force balance on a half-droplet: internal pressure acts on the projected area πR², surface tension acts along the circumference 2πR.
Droplet and Bubble Pressure

From \(\sum F_x = 0\): \(\pi R^2 \Delta p - 2\pi R \Upsilon = 0\)

\[ \Delta p_{\text{droplet}} = \frac{2\Upsilon}{R} \qquad \Delta p_{\text{bubble}} = \frac{4\Upsilon}{R} \]

A bubble has two surfaces (inner and outer), hence double the droplet pressure.

Δp = pinternal − patmosphere R = radius Υ = surface tension

Capillarity

Left: wetting liquid (water in glass) — adhesion > cohesion → concave meniscus, liquid rises. Right: non-wetting liquid (mercury) — cohesion > adhesion → convex meniscus, liquid falls.
Capillary Height

Balancing surface tension (vertical component) against the fluid column weight:

\[ h = \frac{2\Upsilon \cos\theta}{\gamma R} \]

Positive (rises) for \(\theta < 90°\) (wetting); negative (falls) for \(\theta > 90°\) (non-wetting).

h = capillary rise height θ = contact angle Υ = surface tension γ = ρg = specific weight R = tube radius
Example — Capillary Rise

Water–air–glass (\(R = 1\) mm, \(\theta \approx 0°\), \(\Upsilon = 0.073\) N/m, \(\rho = 1000\) kg/m³):

\[ h = \frac{2(0.073)(\cos 0°)}{(1000)(9.81)(0.001)} = 0.015\;\text{m} = 1.5\;\text{cm (rises)} \]

Mercury–air–glass (\(\theta = 130°\), \(\Upsilon = 0.48\) N/m, \(\rho = 13{,}600\) kg/m³):

\[ h = \frac{2(0.48)(\cos 130°)}{(13{,}600)(9.81)(0.001)} = -0.0046\;\text{m} = -0.46\;\text{cm (falls)} \]

These capillary effects must be corrected when using small-diameter tubes for pressure measurements (Ch 2).

Ideal Gas Law

Ideal Gas Law

\[ p = \rho R T \]

Relates pressure, density, and absolute temperature for an ideal gas. \(R\) is the specific gas constant (gas-dependent).

p = absolute pressure [Pa] ρ = density [kg/m³] R = specific gas constant [J/(kg·K)] T = absolute temperature [K]
Example — Ideal Gas Law

Problem: 8 m³ of oxygen at 80 kPa and 15°C is compressed to 25 kPa at constant T. Find the new density and volume. (\(R_{O_2} = 259.8\) J/(kg·K))

Solution

Step 1: Initial density: \(\rho_1 = \frac{p_1}{RT_1} = \frac{80{,}000}{259.8 \times 288} = 1.069\;\text{kg/m}^3\)

Step 2: At constant T: \(\rho_2 = \rho_1 \cdot \frac{p_2}{p_1} = 1.069 \times \frac{25}{80} = 0.334\;\text{kg/m}^3\)

Step 3: Mass conserved: \(m = \rho_1 V_1 = 1.069 \times 8 = 8.554\;\text{kg}\)

\[ V_2 = \frac{m}{\rho_2} = \frac{8.554}{0.334} = \boxed{25.6\;\text{m}^3} \]

Lecture 1.3 · Text Ch 2.10 · Week of May 4th

1.3 — Hydrostatics & Manometers

Many fluid problems do not involve motion at all. Think of water tanks, reservoirs, dams, and hydraulic systems — the fluid sits at rest, yet pressure forces can be enormous. When the fluid velocity is everywhere zero, we say the fluid is in a hydrostatic condition. This lecture covers how pressure distributes itself in a stationary fluid and how we measure it.

Hydrostatics and Pressure

Recall from Lecture 1.2 that pressure is defined as the normal force per unit area: \(p = dF/dA\). In a moving fluid, both normal forces (pressure) and shear forces (viscosity) act on fluid elements. In a static fluid there is no relative motion between layers — no velocity gradient — so by Newton’s law of viscosity (\(\tau = \mu\,du/dy\)), shear stress is identically zero.

★ Key Insight

In a static fluid, the only surface force is pressure (normal force). All shear stresses vanish because there is no fluid motion.

Characteristic of Pressure

To understand how pressure behaves at a point, consider a small triangular (wedge-shaped) fluid element in static equilibrium. The element has width \(b\) into the page, with faces experiencing pressures \(p_x\), \(p_z\), and \(p_n\) (on the inclined face at angle \(\theta\)).

Wedge-shaped fluid element: force balance proves pressure is equal in all directions at a point (Slide 4)

Derivation: Pressure at a Point

Step 1 — x-direction:

\[\sum F_x = 0 \implies p_x\,b\,\Delta z - p_n\,b\,\Delta s\,\sin\theta = 0\]

From the geometry, \(\Delta s\,\sin\theta = \Delta z\), so:

\[p_x = p_n \tag{1}\]

Step 2 — z-direction:

\[\sum F_z = 0 \implies p_z\,b\,\Delta x - p_n\,b\,\Delta s\,\cos\theta - \tfrac{1}{2}\rho g\,b\,\Delta x\,\Delta z = 0\]

Using \(\Delta s\,\cos\theta = \Delta x\):

\[p_z = p_n + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho g\,\Delta z \tag{2}\]

Step 3 — Shrink to a point: Since \(\theta\) is arbitrary and \(\Delta z \to 0\), the weight term vanishes:

\[\boxed{p_x = p_z = p_n = p} \tag{3}\]

Pressure Is a Scalar

Pressure at a point in a static fluid is the same in all directions — it is a scalar, not a vector. It is a thermodynamic property like temperature and density. A body in contact with a static fluid experiences a normal force at each point due to pressure.

Pascal’s Law

A pressure change occurring anywhere in a confined incompressible fluid is transmitted throughout the fluid such that the same change occurs everywhere. This is the foundation of all hydraulic machinery.

Static Pressure Variation

Consider a small cubic control volume of static fluid. Applying force balance in each coordinate direction reveals the fundamental pressure distribution law.

Force balance on an infinitesimal control volume in a static fluid (Slide 8)

Derivation: Hydrostatic Pressure Equation

Sum forces in the \(z\)-direction on the CV (\(\Delta A = \Delta x\,\Delta y\)):

\[\left(p - \frac{\partial p}{\partial z}\frac{\Delta z}{2}\right)\!\Delta A - \left(p + \frac{\partial p}{\partial z}\frac{\Delta z}{2}\right)\!\Delta A - \gamma(\Delta A\,\Delta z) = 0\]

Simplifying gives:

\[\frac{dp}{dz} = -\gamma \qquad \text{and} \qquad \frac{dp}{dx} = \frac{dp}{dy} = 0\]

Hydrostatic Pressure Gradient

\[\frac{dp}{dz} = -\gamma = -\rho g\]
\(p\) = pressure [Pa] \(z\) = vertical coordinate (positive upward) [m] \(\gamma\) = specific weight [N/m³] \(\rho\) = density [kg/m³] \(g\) = gravitational acceleration [m/s²]

★ Three Principles of Hydrostatic Pressure

1. No pressure change in the horizontal direction.
2. In the vertical direction, pressure changes proportionally to \(\rho g\,\Delta z\).
3. Pressure is equal in all directions at a point.

Incompressible Fluid: Pressure–Depth Relation

For an incompressible liquid (constant \(\gamma\)) with no significant gravity variation, integrate \(dp = -\gamma\,dz\) from point 1 to point 2:

Pressure–Depth Relation (Incompressible)

\[p_2 - p_1 = -\gamma(z_2 - z_1)\]

Equivalently:

\[z_1 + \frac{p_1}{\gamma} = z_2 + \frac{p_2}{\gamma}\]
\(p_1, p_2\) = pressures at points 1 and 2 [Pa] \(z_1, z_2\) = elevations [m] \(\gamma = \rho g\) = specific weight [N/m³]

In a continuously distributed uniform static fluid, pressure varies only with vertical distance and is independent of container shape. Pressure is the same at all points on a given horizontal plane in the same uniform fluid.

Points at the same depth in the same continuous fluid have equal pressure, but \(p_A = p_B = p_C \neq p_D\) since D is in mercury (Slide 10)

★ Exam Warning

Points at the same depth have equal pressure only if they are in the same continuous fluid. If a different fluid separates them, pressures are NOT equal even at the same elevation.

Absolute Pressure, Gage Pressure, and Vacuum

Relationships between absolute, gage, and vacuum pressure (Slide 13)

Pressure Reference Definitions

\[p_{\text{gage}} = p_{\text{absolute}} - p_{\text{atm}}\] \[p_{\text{vacuum}} = p_{\text{atm}} - p_{\text{absolute}}\]
\(p_{\text{absolute}}\) = pressure from absolute zero [Pa] \(p_{\text{atm}}\) ≈ 101,325 Pa at sea level \(p_{\text{gage}}\) = pressure above atmosphere \(p_{\text{vacuum}}\) = pressure below atmosphere

Absolute pressure is measured from absolute zero (perfect vacuum). Gage pressure is measured from local atmosphere — what most gauges read. Vacuum pressure applies when absolute pressure is below atmospheric.

Pressure Head

Since \(p_{\text{gage}} = \gamma h\) for an incompressible fluid, any pressure can be expressed as the height of a liquid column:

Pressure Head

\[h_{\text{liquid}} = \frac{p_{\text{gage}}}{\gamma}\]
\(h\) = height of liquid column [m] \(p_{\text{gage}}\) = gage pressure [Pa] \(\gamma\) = specific weight [N/m³]

Example: Pressure Head Comparison

To produce a gage pressure of 50 kPa:

Water (\(\gamma_w = 9810\) N/m³): \(h = 50\times10^3 / 9810 = 5.10\) m

Mercury (\(\gamma_{Hg} = 133{,}100\) N/m³): \(h = 50\times10^3 / 133{,}100 = 0.376\) m

Mercury needs a much shorter column because it is 13.6× denser — this is why mercury manometers are compact.

Hydrostatic Pressure in Oceans and Atmosphere

Pressure above and below the free surface (Slide 14)

Taking the free surface as \(z = 0\) with pressure \(p_a\): moving upward by height \(b\), \(p \approx p_a - b\gamma_{\text{air}}\). Moving downward by depth \(h\), \(p \approx p_a + h\gamma_{\text{water}}\). Be careful with signs.

Example 2.1 — Lake Pressure

Problem: Newfound Lake, max depth 60 m, atmospheric pressure 91 kPa. Find absolute pressure at maximum depth.

Show Solution

Given: \(h = 60\) m, \(p_a = 91\) kPa, \(\gamma_{\text{water}} = 9790\) N/m³

\[p_{\max} = p_a - \gamma z = 91{,}000 - (9790)(-60) = 678{,}400\text{ Pa}\] \[\boxed{p_{\max} \approx 678\text{ kPa}}\]

Tip: Always use pascals in the formula, convert to kPa at the end.

Example — Pipe AB Force on Cap

Problem: Water fills pipe AB. Absolute pressure at A = 400 kPa, atmospheric = 101 kPa, pipe inner diameter = 50 mm. B is 0.3 m above A. Find resultant force on cap at B.

Show Solution

Step 1: Pressure at B (B is higher, so \(z_A - z_B = -0.3\) m):

\[p_B = p_A + \rho_w g(z_A - z_B) = 400 + (1000)(9.81)(-0.3)/1000 = 397.06\text{ kPa}\]

Step 2: Net force on cap (inside: water at \(p_B\), outside: atmosphere):

\[F_B = (p_B - p_{\text{atm}})\pi r^2 = (397.06 - 101)\times10^3 \times \pi(0.025)^2\] \[\boxed{F_B = 581.3\text{ N}}\]

Compressible Fluid: Atmospheric Pressure

For gases, density varies with altitude — we cannot use \(p_2 - p_1 = -\gamma(z_2 - z_1)\). Instead, combine \(dp = -\gamma\,dz\) with the ideal gas law \(\gamma = pg/(RT)\):

Derivation: Compressible Pressure

\[\frac{dp}{p} = -\frac{g}{RT}\,dz\]

This separable ODE requires knowing how \(T\) varies with \(z\). Two cases: linear lapse rate (troposphere) and constant temperature (stratosphere).

Troposphere Pressure (0 ≤ z < 11 km)

Temperature: \(T = T_0 - Bz\), with \(T_0 = 288.16\) K, \(B = 0.00650\) K/m.

\[p = p_0\!\left(1 - \frac{Bz}{T_0}\right)^{\!g/(RB)}\]

where \(g/(RB) \approx 5.26\) for air.

\(p_0\) = sea-level pressure = 101,350 Pa \(T_0\) = 288.16 K \(B\) = 0.00650 K/m (lapse rate) \(R\) = 287 J/(kg·K) for air

Isothermal Atmosphere

\[p = p_0\,e^{-gz/(RT_0)}\]
Applies in stratosphere (11–20.1 km) at \(T \approx -56.5\)°C Also used as quick troposphere approximation (~4% error at 5 km)

★ Tip: Use Absolute p and T

In gas law calculations, pressure must be in Pascals (not kPa) and temperature in Kelvin (not °C). Mixing gage/Celsius is the most common error.

Specific Weight of Common Fluids

Fluid \(\gamma\) [lbf/ft³] \(\gamma\) [N/m³]
Air (1 atm)0.075211.8
Ethyl Alcohol49.27,733
SAE 30 Oil55.58,720
Water62.49,790
Seawater64.010,050
Glycerin78.712,360
Carbon Tetrachloride99.115,570
Mercury846133,100

All values at 68°F = 20°C

Hydraulic Machinery

Pascal’s Law in action: a small force on a small piston produces a large force on a large piston. This is the principle behind hydraulic jacks, brakes, presses, and lifts.

Hydraulic force multiplication (Slide 24)

Hydraulic Force Multiplication

\[\frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2} \implies F_2 = F_1\,\frac{A_2}{A_1}\] \[\text{Mechanical advantage} = \frac{F_2}{F_1} = \frac{A_2}{A_1}\]
\(F_1\) = applied force [N] \(F_2\) = output force [N] \(A_1, A_2\) = piston areas [m²]

Manometry

A manometer measures pressure using liquid columns. Since \(dp/dz = -\gamma\), measuring column height directly gives pressure difference.

Barometer

Barometer: \(p_{\text{atm}} = \gamma_{\text{liquid}}\,h\) when \(p_{\text{vap}} \approx 0\) (Slide 26)

Barometer Equation

\[p_{\text{atm}} = \gamma_{\text{liquid}}\,h \quad (\text{when } p_{\text{vap}} \approx 0)\]
\(h\) = liquid column height [m] \(\gamma_{\text{liquid}}\) = specific weight of manometer fluid [N/m³]

Multi-Fluid Manometer

Multi-fluid manometer: sum pressure changes through each layer (Slide 27)

General Manometer Rule

\[p_n - p_1 = \sum_{\text{down}} \gamma_i\,|h_i| \;-\; \sum_{\text{up}} \gamma_i\,|h_i|\]
"Down" = lower elevation → add \(\gamma h\) "Up" = higher elevation → subtract \(\gamma h\) Jump across at same level in same fluid

U-Tube and Inclined-Tube Manometers

Left: U-tube manometer. Right: inclined-tube — tilting amplifies readable length for small pressure differences (Slide 30)

Differential Manometer

Measures pressure difference across a flow device (valve, orifice). For a U-tube differential manometer:

Differential Manometer

\[p_a - p_b = (\rho_2 - \rho_1)\,g\,h\]
\(h\) = gauge fluid height difference [m] \(\rho_2\) = gauge fluid density (e.g. mercury) [kg/m³] \(\rho_1\) = working fluid density [kg/m³]

★ Common Student Error

In the differential manometer, note the density difference \((\rho_2 - \rho_1)\). Forgetting to subtract the working fluid density is a very common mistake and a serious error when both fluids are liquids.

Example 2.4 — Multi-Fluid Manometer

Problem: Gage B reads 87 kPa at point A in a water flow. Manometer has water (down 5 cm), mercury (up 7 cm), SAE 30 oil (up 6 cm). Find \(p_A\). Fluids at 20°C.

Show Solution

Properties: \(\gamma_w = 9790\) N/m³, \(\gamma_m = 133{,}100\) N/m³, \(\gamma_o = 8720\) N/m³

Method: Start at A, go "down" then "up," jumping across at the mercury meniscus:

\[p_A + \gamma_w(0.05) - \gamma_m(0.07) - \gamma_o(0.06) = p_B\] \[p_A + 490 - 9317 - 523 = 87{,}000\] \[\boxed{p_A \approx 96.4\text{ kPa}}\]

Note: The 5-figure intermediate result is unrealistic — data are known to ~3 significant figures.

★ Manometer Problem Strategy

1. Start at a point of known pressure.
2. Walk through: going down adds \(\gamma h\), going up subtracts \(\gamma h\).
3. At each fluid interface, "jump across" — pressures equal at same level in same fluid.
4. End at the unknown and solve.

Equation Sheet

All key equations from MAAE 2300 — grows as chapters are added

Ch 1 — Fluid Properties & Pressure

Density (Continuum Definition)
\[ \rho = \lim_{\delta V \to \delta V^*} \frac{\delta m}{\delta V} \]

What it means: Density is the mass per unit volume, defined at the smallest volume element \(\delta V^*\) where molecular fluctuations average out and a stable macroscopic value emerges.

Origin: Derived from the continuum assumption — at volumes larger than \(\delta V^* \sim 10^{-9}\) mm³ (containing ~\(3 \times 10^7\) molecules of air at STP), density is a smooth function of position, enabling differential calculus.

When to use: Any problem requiring fluid density as a point property. Underlies every governing equation in the course — continuity, momentum, energy.

When NOT to use: Does not apply at molecular scales (e.g., rarefied gas dynamics where mean free path ≈ characteristic length). Also breaks down at macroscopic scales where spatial non-uniformity matters (use local density instead of bulk average).

Use cases: "Find the density of water at 20°C" → look up \(\rho = 998\) kg/m³. "Is the continuum assumption valid?" → check if the problem length scale ≫ mean free path.

\[ \rho = \lim_{\delta V \to \delta V^*} \frac{\delta m}{\delta V} \]

Mass per unit volume at the continuum scale. Valid when problem length scale ≫ mean free path (~\(10^{-9}\) mm³ threshold).

\[ \rho = \lim_{\delta V \to \delta V^*} \frac{\delta m}{\delta V} \]

💡 Insider Tips

  • Every long-answer starts with a CV sketch. Draw the control volume, label all inlets/outlets, show pressure forces and the reaction force you're solving for. Partial marks come from this.
  • Bernoulli + Continuity are always paired. You'll never use Bernoulli alone — continuity gives you the velocity relationship, then Bernoulli connects pressures/elevations.
  • Hydrostatic pressure on a vertical surface = ρg·yc·A. The centroid depth yc is at half the water height. This substitution appears in every momentum problem involving open-channel flow.
  • Sign convention matters. Pick a positive direction, define FR as the force on the fluid (not the gate), then flip at the end. Getting this backwards is the #1 error.
  • Mass conservation ≠ volume conservation. Q1c proves this — the air and water have different densities, so equal volume flow rates give very different mass flow rates (ratio ≈ ρair/ρwater ≈ 1.2/1000).
  • Manometer reading: trace from one end to the other. Go step by step: +ρgh going down, −ρgh going up, switching ρ at each fluid interface. Don't try to shortcut it.

🧭 Problem Type → Strategy

Problem looks like…Use…Key equation
"Find the force on a gate/plate/nozzle"Linear Momentum (RTT) + Bernoulli\(\sum \vec{F} = \sum_{\text{out}} \dot{m}\vec{V} - \sum_{\text{in}} \dot{m}\vec{V}\)
"Find the flow rate" with two pipe sectionsBernoulli + Continuity + manometer\(\frac{p_1}{\gamma}+\frac{V_1^2}{2g}+z_1 = \frac{p_2}{\gamma}+\frac{V_2^2}{2g}+z_2\)
"Find the air/gas outflow" from a tank filling with liquidMass Conservation (RTT) with density ratio\(\dot{m}_{\text{air}} = \dot{m}_{\text{water}} \cdot \frac{\rho_{\text{air}}}{\rho_{\text{water}}}\)
"Velocity variation along a streamline" through a contractionContinuity (\(A_1 V_1 = A_2 V_2\)) — velocity increases as area decreases\(Q = AV = \text{const}\)
"Do pressure forces affect angular momentum?"Yes — pressure acts normal to surfaces but CAN create a net torque about an axis\(\sum \vec{M} = \sum_{\text{out}} (\vec{r}\times\vec{V})\dot{m} - \sum_{\text{in}} (\vec{r}\times\vec{V})\dot{m}\)

✅ Topic Checklist

Check off topics as you review them — state is saved in your browser.

⚠️ Common Traps

  1. Forgetting the hydrostatic pressure term in momentum. The momentum equation gives \(\sum F = \dot{m}\Delta V\). The forces include both pressure forces on the CV surfaces and the reaction force. The pressure force on a vertical water surface is \(\frac{1}{2}\rho g w y^2\), not just \(p \cdot A\).
  2. Getting the sign of FR backwards. Define \(F_{Rx}\) as the force exerted on the fluid by the gate. After solving, if the result is positive, the actual force on the gate points in the opposite direction. State clearly what your sign means.
  3. Wrong manometer reading. Mixing up which direction adds or subtracts pressure. Rule: going DOWN in a fluid → pressure INCREASES (+ρgh). Going UP → pressure DECREASES (−ρgh). Switch ρ at each interface.
  4. Continuity ratio for circular pipes. \(V_1/V_2 = (D_2/D_1)^2\), NOT \(D_2/D_1\). The area scales with diameter squared.
  5. Assuming mass flow = volume flow. Q1c tests this directly. \(\dot{m} = \rho Q\), and since \(\rho_{\text{air}} \neq \rho_{\text{water}}\), equal volume flow rates give very different mass flow rates.

Sample Midterm II — Worked Solutions

Midterm 2 — June 11, 2026 · Ch 3–5 (Bernoulli, Fluid Dynamics, RTT) · 3 MCQ (20 marks) + 2 Long Answer (80 marks)
⬅ Back to Midterm 2 Prep overview

Question 1a — Angular Momentum & Pressure Forces (5 marks)

Statement: Consider the validity of this statement: "Pressure forces do not contribute to changes in angular momentum since they are non-directional forces (acting normal to any surfaces) and should not be included when conserving the angular momentum of a control volume."
🧠 Thought process

The claim says pressure is "non-directional" — this is wrong. Pressure produces a force \(\vec{F} = p \cdot A \cdot \hat{n}\) that acts in a specific direction (normal to each surface). While the scalar pressure \(p\) is isotropic, the resulting force has a direction. If this force has a moment arm \(\vec{r}\) about an axis, it creates torque \(\vec{r} \times \vec{F} \neq 0\). Therefore pressure absolutely contributes to angular momentum changes.

✅ Answer: (b) The statement is invalid

Pressure forces are directional — they act normal to surfaces and can create torque about any axis when they have a nonzero moment arm. They must be included in the angular momentum equation for a control volume.

★ Tip: "Pressure is a scalar" ≠ "pressure force is non-directional." The force vector is \(\vec{F}_p = -p\hat{n}\,dA\), which has magnitude AND direction.

Question 1b — Velocity Variation Along a Streamline (5 marks)

Statement: Consider the flow depicted in the figure. If the flow is incompressible, then the velocity variation of a particle moving along the streamline going through point A will follow which curve?
Streamlines converging toward a circular body — velocity graph options a through d
🧠 Thought process

The streamlines converge from left to right toward a circular body, then diverge past it. By continuity (\(A_1 V_1 = A_2 V_2\)), as the cross-sectional area between streamlines decreases, velocity must increase. Approaching the body (A → B), the streamlines squeeze together so velocity increases. After passing the body, streamlines spread again and velocity decreases back.

At point A the velocity is \(V_A\). It must increase smoothly toward the narrowest point (near the body) and then decrease. This matches curve "a" — starts at \(V_A\), rises to a peak near the body, then drops.

✅ Answer: (a) curve "a"

The velocity increases as streamlines converge (area decreases), peaks near the body's narrowest cross-section, then decreases as streamlines diverge. Curve "a" is the only one showing this bell-shaped profile starting and ending near \(V_A\).

★ Tip: When streamlines get closer together → flow speeds up. When they spread apart → flow slows down. This is a direct visual application of \(Q = AV = \text{const}\).

Question 1c — Cylindrical Tank Mass Conservation (10 marks)

Statement: A cylindrical tank has two connecting pipes of equal radius \(R\). The lower pipe provides water inflow (\(\dot{m}_{\text{water}} = 10\) kg/s) while the upper pipe is used for air outflow. The pressure inside the tank above the water surface equals one atmosphere. The tank height is \(50R\) with unknown radius. The tank is half full. Find the air mass outflow.
Cylindrical tank with water inflow (bottom) and air outflow (top)
🧠 Thought process

This is a mass conservation problem. Water flows in at the bottom, raising the water level. As the water level rises, it compresses the air above it and pushes air out the top pipe. Key insight: the volume of water entering per second equals the volume of air leaving per second (incompressible water, atmospheric-pressure air). But mass flow rate = ρ × Q, so the mass outflow of air is much smaller because \(\rho_{\text{air}} \ll \rho_{\text{water}}\).

📋 Formulas Needed

  1. Mass conservation (CV): \(\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_{CV}\rho\,dV + \int_{CS}\rho(\vec{V}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA = 0\)
  2. Incompressible volume balance: \(Q_{\text{in}} = Q_{\text{out}}\) → volume flow rate of water in = volume flow rate of air out
  3. Mass flow rate: \(\dot{m} = \rho Q\)

Solution

1
Volumetric flow rate of water in
Since water is incompressible, the volume flow rate entering is: \[Q_{\text{water}} = \frac{\dot{m}_{\text{water}}}{\rho_{\text{water}}} = \frac{10\text{ kg/s}}{1000\text{ kg/m}^3} = 0.01\text{ m}^3\text{/s}\]
2
Volume balance
As the water level rises by \(dh\), the water occupies volume \(A_{\text{tank}}\,dh\) and displaces the same volume of air from the tank. Therefore the volumetric flow rate of air leaving equals the volumetric flow rate of water entering: \[Q_{\text{air}} = Q_{\text{water}} = 0.01\text{ m}^3\text{/s}\]
3
Air mass outflow
At atmospheric pressure, \(\rho_{\text{air}} \approx 1.2\text{ kg/m}^3\): \[\dot{m}_{\text{air}} = \rho_{\text{air}} \cdot Q_{\text{air}} = 1.2 \times 0.01 = 0.012\text{ kg/s}\]
✅ Answer: (d) 0.012 kg/s
★ Tip: The tank radius is irrelevant — a classic distractor. The volume balance doesn't depend on the tank dimensions, only on the fact that incompressible water in = air displaced out. The mass ratio is simply \(\rho_{\text{air}}/\rho_{\text{water}} \approx 1.2/1000\), so 10 kg/s of water → 0.012 kg/s of air.

Question 2 — Sluice Gate Force (40 marks)

Statement: A sluice gate controls flow rate in a channel. A force is exerted on the gate due to the difference between water heights \(y_1\) (upstream) and \(y_2\) (downstream) and the flow velocities \(V_1\) and \(V_2\). The width of the gate into the page is \(w\). Wall shear stresses are negligible; assume steady, uniform flow at locations 1 and 2. Develop a relationship for the force \(F_R\) acting on the sluice gate as a function of \(y_1\), \(y_2\), \(\dot{m}\), \(g\), \(w\), and \(\rho\).
Sluice gate in an open channel — upstream depth y₁, downstream depth y₂
🧠 Thought process

This is a linear momentum + Bernoulli problem. The clue is "find the force on a gate" — that means momentum equation. But we also need Bernoulli to relate the velocities and pressures upstream and downstream. The strategy is: (1) Bernoulli between the free surfaces, (2) Continuity for velocity relation, (3) Momentum equation for the force.

The control volume is the water body between the upstream and downstream cross-sections, bounded by the channel bottom, free surfaces, and the gate surface.

📋 Formulas Needed

  1. Bernoulli's Equation: \(\frac{p_1}{\rho g} + \frac{V_1^2}{2g} + z_1 = \frac{p_2}{\rho g} + \frac{V_2^2}{2g} + z_2\)
  2. Continuity: \(A_1 V_1 = A_2 V_2 \implies (wy_1)V_1 = (wy_2)V_2\)
  3. Linear Momentum (x-dir): \(\sum F_x = \dot{m}V_2 - \dot{m}V_1\)
  4. Hydrostatic pressure force on vertical surface: \(F_p = \rho g \frac{y}{2} \cdot (wy) = \frac{1}{2}\rho g w y^2\)

Solution

1
Apply Bernoulli between the free surfaces (points 1 and 2)
Take point 1 at the upstream free surface and point 2 at the downstream free surface. Both are at atmospheric pressure (\(p_1 = p_2 = p_{\text{atm}}\)). Take the channel bottom as the elevation reference, so \(z_1 = y_1\) and \(z_2 = y_2\): \[\frac{V_1^2}{2g} + y_1 = \frac{V_2^2}{2g} + y_2\] \[\boxed{V_2^2 - V_1^2 = 2g(y_1 - y_2)} \quad \cdots (1)\]
2
Apply Continuity
For steady, incompressible flow with a single inlet and outlet: \[A_1 V_1 = A_2 V_2 \implies (wy_1)V_1 = (wy_2)V_2\] The mass flow rate is \(\dot{m} = \rho A V\), so: \[V_1 = \frac{\dot{m}}{\rho w y_1}, \quad V_2 = \frac{\dot{m}}{\rho w y_2} \quad \cdots (2)\]
3
Set up the momentum equation
Choose the control volume as the water body bounded by the upstream cross-section (area \(wy_1\)), downstream cross-section (area \(wy_2\)), the channel bottom, the free surfaces, and the inner surface of the sluice gate. The forces in the x-direction are:
  • Upstream pressure force (pushing right): \(P_1 A_1 = \rho g \frac{y_1}{2}(wy_1) = \frac{1}{2}\rho g w y_1^2\)
  • Downstream pressure force (pushing left): \(P_2 A_2 = \rho g \frac{y_2}{2}(wy_2) = \frac{1}{2}\rho g w y_2^2\)
  • Gate reaction force \(F_{Rx}\) (acts on the fluid, assumed pointing left/negative)
  • Wall shear: negligible (given)
The linear momentum equation in the x-direction: \[\sum F_x = \dot{m}V_2 - \dot{m}V_1\] \[-F_{Rx} + \frac{1}{2}\rho g w y_1^2 - \frac{1}{2}\rho g w y_2^2 = \dot{m}(V_2 - V_1)\]
4
Solve for FRx
Rearranging: \[\boxed{F_{Rx} = \dot{m}(V_1 - V_2) + \frac{w}{2}\rho g(y_1^2 - y_2^2)}\] where \(V_1 = \frac{\dot{m}}{\rho w y_1}\) and \(V_2 = \frac{\dot{m}}{\rho w y_2}\) from Eq. (2).
5
Substitute velocity expressions (expanded form)
Substituting the continuity relations into the force expression: \[F_{Rx} = \dot{m}\left(\frac{\dot{m}}{\rho w y_1} - \frac{\dot{m}}{\rho w y_2}\right) + \frac{w}{2}\rho g(y_1^2 - y_2^2)\] Or equivalently, using the Bernoulli-derived velocity expressions from Eq. (1) and (2): \[F_{Rx} = \dot{m}\left(\frac{y_2}{y_1} - 1\right)\sqrt{\frac{2g(y_1 - y_2)}{1 - y_2^2/y_1^2}} + \frac{w}{2}\rho g(y_1^2 - y_2^2)\]
📦 Final Answer
\[F_{Rx} = \dot{m}(V_1 - V_2) + \frac{w}{2}\rho g(y_1^2 - y_2^2)\]
Momentum contribution + Hydrostatic pressure contribution
★ Tips & tricks:
• The force has two parts: momentum change (\(\dot{m}\Delta V\)) and net pressure force (\(\frac{w}{2}\rho g \Delta(y^2)\)). Most students forget the pressure term — it's the hydrostatic force difference between the two cross-sections.
• \(F_{Rx}\) is the force the gate exerts on the fluid. The force on the gate is equal and opposite (Newton's 3rd law). Since \(y_1 > y_2\), the force on the gate points downstream (to the right).
• The problem says "develop a relationship" — this means a symbolic expression. Don't plug in numbers.
🔗 Concept bridge: Bernoulli (Ch 3) → Continuity / RTT–Mass (Ch 5, §3.3) → Linear Momentum / RTT–Momentum (Ch 5, §3.4) → Hydrostatic pressure on vertical surfaces (Ch 1–2, review)

Question 3 — Downward Pipe Flow with Manometer (40 marks)

Statement: Water flows steadily downward in the pipe shown in the figure with negligible losses. Determine the flow rate. The upper pipe has diameter 1.2 m, the lower pipe has diameter 1 m. A U-tube manometer with oil (SG = 0.7) connects the two pipe sections. The upper manometer column height \(h_1 = 1.5\) m, the vertical distance between pipe centres is 2 m, and the lower manometer column height \(h_2 = 2\) m.
Downward pipe flow with U-tube oil manometer (SG = 0.7)
🧠 Thought process

This is a Bernoulli + Continuity + Manometer problem. "Find the flow rate" with two pipe diameters and a manometer connecting them. Strategy: (1) Use Bernoulli between points 1 and 2 (the two pipe centres), (2) Use continuity to relate \(V_1\) and \(V_2\), (3) Use the manometer to find the pressure difference \(p_2 - p_1\), (4) Combine everything to solve for \(V_2\), then compute \(Q = A_2 V_2\).

📋 Formulas Needed

  1. Bernoulli: \(\frac{p_1}{\gamma} + \frac{V_1^2}{2g} + z_1 = \frac{p_2}{\gamma} + \frac{V_2^2}{2g} + z_2\)
  2. Continuity: \(A_1 V_1 = A_2 V_2\)
  3. Manometer pressure trace: step-by-step through the U-tube
  4. Volume flow rate: \(Q = AV = \frac{\pi}{4}D^2 V\)

Solution

1
Write Bernoulli between points 1 (upper pipe) and 2 (lower pipe)
Let \(z_1 - z_2 = 2\) m (upper pipe is 2 m above lower pipe). With no losses: \[\frac{p_1}{\gamma} + \frac{V_1^2}{2g} + z_1 = \frac{p_2}{\gamma} + \frac{V_2^2}{2g} + z_2 \quad \cdots (1)\]
2
Apply Continuity
\[A_1 V_1 = A_2 V_2 \implies \frac{\pi}{4}(1.2)^2 V_1 = \frac{\pi}{4}(1.0)^2 V_2\] \[V_1 = \frac{(1.0)^2}{(1.2)^2} V_2 = 0.694\,V_2 \quad \cdots (2)\]
3
Read the manometer — trace pressure from point 1 to point 2
Starting at point 1, trace through the manometer step by step. The open end of the manometer is at the top, and the manometer fluid is oil with \(\gamma_{\text{oil}} = 0.7\gamma\):
  • At point 1: pressure = \(p_1\)
  • Go down \(h_1 = 1.5\) m in water: pressure increases by \(\gamma h_1\) → \(p_1 + \gamma h_1\)
  • Cross into oil, go up \(h_1 = 1.5\) m in oil: pressure decreases by \(\gamma_{\text{oil}} h_1 = 0.7\gamma h_1\)
  • Continue up \(h_2 = 2\) m in water on the other side to reach point 2: pressure decreases by \(\gamma h_2\)
Therefore: \[p_2 = p_1 + \gamma h_1 - 0.7\gamma h_1 - \gamma h_2\] Wait — let me be more careful. From the figure, the manometer setup is:
  • \(p_1 = \gamma h_1\) (at point 1, the pressure is due to the water column above)
  • \(p_2 = \gamma_{\text{oil}} h_1 + \gamma h_2\) (at point 2, the pressure comes from oil column + water column)
The pressure difference: \[\frac{p_2 - p_1}{\gamma} = (0.7h_1 + h_2) - h_1 = h_2 - 0.3h_1\] \[\frac{p_2 - p_1}{\gamma} = 2 - 0.3(1.5) = 2 - 0.45 = 1.55\text{ m} \quad \cdots (3)\]
4
Substitute into Bernoulli and solve
Rearranging Eq. (1): \[z_1 - z_2 = \frac{p_2 - p_1}{\gamma} + \frac{V_2^2}{2g} - \frac{V_1^2}{2g}\] Substituting Eqs. (2) and (3): \[2 = 1.55 + \frac{V_2^2}{2(9.81)}\left(1 - (0.694)^2\right)\] \[0.45 = \frac{V_2^2}{19.62}(1 - 0.4816) = \frac{V_2^2}{19.62}(0.5184)\] \[V_2^2 = \frac{0.45 \times 19.62}{0.5184} = 17.03\] \[V_2 = 4.13\text{ m/s}\]
5
Compute the flow rate
\[Q = A_2 V_2 = \frac{\pi}{4}(1\text{ m})^2 \times 4.13\text{ m/s}\] \[Q = 0.7854 \times 4.13 = 3.24\text{ m}^3\text{/s}\]
📦 Final Answer
\[Q = 3.24 \text{ m}^3\text{/s}\]
★ Tips & tricks:
• When reading a manometer, always trace from one known point to the other: +ρgh going down, −ρgh going up, changing ρ at each fluid interface.
• The continuity ratio \(V_1/V_2 = (D_2/D_1)^2\) — for circular pipes, it's the diameter ratio squared (not the radius).
• Don't forget that \(z_1 - z_2 = +2\) m because flow goes downward — the upper pipe is at the higher elevation. This is a free energy source that helps the flow.
🔗 Concept bridge: Bernoulli (Ch 3) → Continuity / RTT–Mass (Ch 5, §3.3) → Manometry (Ch 1, §2.10 review)

Key patterns

  • Bernoulli appears in 80% of the exam (both long answers) — always paired with continuity
  • Continuity is the universal first step — used in every single question
  • Momentum equation = highest-value question (40 marks) — learn the CV setup cold
  • MCQs are conceptual, not computational — test understanding of why, not how to calculate
  • Manometry is still tested despite being Ch 1 material — review the step-by-step trace method

Time allocation suggestion (if 75 min)

  • MCQs (Q1a–c): 12 min total — don't overthink, mark and move on
  • Q2 (sluice gate): 30 min — careful CV sketch, then steady algebra
  • Q3 (pipe flow): 28 min — manometer reading is the tricky part

Ch 1 — Fluid Properties & Pressure

Establishes the foundational definitions and assumptions that underpin every equation in the course — what a fluid is, how we treat it mathematically, and the three branches we will study.

Classification of Matter
What:
Matter classified as solid, liquid, gas, or plasma based on molecular bonding and response to shear stress.
Why:
The defining property of a fluid is that it cannot resist shear stress — it deforms continuously. Solids resist shear by deforming to equilibrium.
How:
Liquids have constant volume/density and form a free surface. Gases expand to fill their container and have no definite volume. Both are fluids.
Trap:
Don't confuse "cannot resist shear" with "has no viscosity." Fluids still resist shear through viscous effects — they just never reach static equilibrium under shear.
The Continuum Assumption
What:
Treat fluid properties as smooth, continuous functions of position rather than tracking individual molecules.
Why:
Enables the use of differential calculus — partial derivatives, integrals, and governing PDEs — for engineering-scale analysis.
How:
\(\rho = \lim_{\delta V \to \delta V^*} \frac{\delta m}{\delta V}\) where \(\delta V^* \sim 10^{-9}\) mm³ gives a stable local density.
Trap:
Fails in rarefied gas flows (high altitude, vacuum systems) where the mean free path approaches the problem's characteristic length.
Branches of Fluid Mechanics
What:
Three branches — hydrostatics (fluids at rest), kinematics (geometry of motion), and fluid dynamics (forces causing acceleration).
Why:
Structures the entire course: Ch 1–2 cover statics, Ch 4 covers kinematics, Ch 5–6 cover dynamics via the Reynolds Transport Theorem.

Classification of matter → shear stress concept reappears in viscosity (Ch 1.2) and Newton's law of viscosity

Continuum assumption → justifies every differential equation in Ch 3–6

Density definition → used directly in hydrostatics (Ch 2), Bernoulli (Ch 3), and RTT (Ch 5)
